runs.text: It's worth pausing to look closely at a tangled hillside covered with all sorts of plants, alive with birds singing in the shrubs, insects darting here and there, and worms working their way through the moist soil — and to realize that these intricate creatures, so unlike one another and so tightly bound together in their dependence on each other, all came into being through forces still operating today. Broadly speaking, those forces are: growth and reproduction; inheritance, which reproduction almost guarantees; variation, arising both indirectly and directly from environmental conditions and from the use or disuse of body parts; a rate of reproduction so rapid that it triggers a struggle for survival, which in turn brings about natural selection — and with it, the branching apart of species and the dying-out of forms that fail to keep pace. So it is that from nature's conflict, from hunger and death, comes the loftiest outcome imaginable: the emergence of higher forms of animal life. There is something magnificent in this way of seeing life — with all its varied capacities — as having been breathed originally into one form or a handful of forms; and in recognizing that even as this planet has kept turning through its cycles under gravity's unchanging pull, life has been unfolding from such a humble start into an endless array of forms, each more beautiful and remarkable than the last, and that this unfolding continues even now.
